children: United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket lifted off Sunday after a nine-month hiatus, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon’s
Leo broadband network. The mission departed Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 12:40 p.m. local time, marking a return for a rocket whose limited flight history has been interrupted by technical problems.
The launch was Vulcan’s fifth since its January 2024 debut and its first since a solid rocket booster malfunction in February. ULA, owned jointly by Boeing
, has struggled to establish a regular launch schedule.
For investors, Vulcan’s return is a step toward relieving launch constraints that have slowed Amazon’s
satellite deployment and threatened ULA’s government revenue. Sustained, reliable flights would help Amazon
build its Starlink competitor while strengthening ULA’s position in commercial and national security launches.
Sunday’s flight opened a series of 38 Vulcan missions booked by Amazon
, following eight launches using ULA’s Atlas V.
Leo has nearly 400 satellites in orbit and regulatory authorization for more than 7,700.
Launch availability remains a concern across the industry. SpaceX
has indicated it intends to retire Falcon 9, while Blue Origin’s New Glenn has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion damaged its sole launch site.
ULA also faces pressure in its defense business. The Space Force suspended Vulcan missions in February, and the Air Force imposed penalties over delays.
deployment timetable. In June, the Federal Communications Commission waived a requirement to place more than 1,600 satellites in orbit by mid-2026. Amazon’s
deadline to complete the constellation remains July 2029.

title: ULA’s Vulcan returns to flight with 40 Amazon internet satellites
